principles: Preserve every N3 question and every teacher-edited or finalised question.
Use direct, concise questions and retain the musical vocabulary taught at each level.
Prefer plausible distractors from the same level and musical category; use earlier-level concepts when those make better alternatives. Never use later-level concepts.
Do not manufacture six questions per concept. Retire redundant descriptions, retaining definitions and listening questions.
Retain recordings, excerpt timings, correct option IDs and typed-answer variants.

analysis.note: Comparison with the pre-language-review snapshot; later curriculum removals are included. These counts describe the teacher-review trajectory, not solely the last editing session.

question.feedback: Augmentation makes a melody’s notes longer, often twice as long, while the beat stays the same.

evidence.supportingText: A theme, melody or rhythm is repeated with every note value lengthened in the same proportion. The material therefore takes longer while retaining its pitch and rhythmic relationships. The underlying pulse remains unchanged even though the transformed idea sounds slower. A common example doubles the note values, so quavers become crotchets while the beat keeps the same speed.

Augmentation is when a phrase is repeated but rhythms double in length. 
The music will sound slower when imitated or repeated.

question.feedback: Melodic inversion reverses the direction of the intervals: an upward third becomes a downward third.

evidence.supportingText: A transformation that reverses the direction of each melodic interval, so an upward interval becomes the corresponding downward interval and vice versa. The term can also describe chord inversion, where a note other than the root appears in the bass. In chord inversion, first inversion places the third in the bass and second inversion places the fifth in the bass.
evidence.verification: Checked against current local Dictionary extended definition and listening cues. No recording audition or comprehensive independent musicological verification claimed.

evidence.supportingText:
Inversion
Each interval changes direction: up becomes down and down becomes up.
Retrograde inversion
The inverted row played in reverse order.
All melodic and harmonic material may be derived from the row. The result is often dissonant and atonal.
Tone-row activity compose and transform
•  1. Create a four-note row — choose four different notes and place them in an order.
•  2. Add a rhythm — give the four notes a clear rhythmic pattern.
•  3. Create the retrograde — write or play the notes in reverse order.
•  4. Create the inversion — reverse the direction of every interval.
•  5. Combine ideas — perform in pairs using different rhythms, retrograde and transposition.
